title: Biosecurity and invasive species
audience: Garden, lawn, irrigation and landscape workers and supervisors who identify, cut, move or dispose of plant material on client sites.
learningOutcomes: Recognise plants that may be invasive, declared or restricted without relying on touch or guesswork.
Stop, avoid spreading suspect plant material and clean tools and footwear where required.
Decide whether material can be moved, composted, chipped or disposed of, and where the decision needs an authority.
Record species uncertainty, the referral and the client's notification.

instruction.heading: Why biosecurity matters on a garden job
instruction.body: Garden and landscape work moves plants, soil, seed and fragments from one property to another. Weeds and pests spread when a seed head is shaken off, a cutting is dropped in a green-waste bin, or a boot carries soil into the next yard. Some plants are declared or restricted because they damage native bushland, waterways, crops or infrastructure. A declared plant may need to be reported, controlled or destroyed under specific rules, and moving it may be an offence. The rules are set by each state and territory and by local government, and their lists differ. Your job on site is to recognise the risk, stop the spread, and refer the decision to someone with the authority to make it. Identifying a plant is not the same as having authority to remove or treat it.

instruction.heading: Recognising suspect plant material
instruction.body: Many weeds look like ordinary garden plants when they are young. Look at the growth habit, leaf arrangement, flower and seed structure, and any unusual sap, thorns or fruit. Compare what you see with a reliable identification source, such as a state or territory weed guide or a qualified botanist, and note any uncertainty. Do not identify a plant by smell or taste, and do not handle sap or fruit with bare hands. If a neighbour, client or sign tells you a plant is a declared weed, take it seriously and stop cutting that plant until you have checked. Photograph the plant and its location with the client's consent, and do not collect seed or cut material for identification unless the process allows it. Keep the plant separate from other green waste so it does not contaminate the rest of the job.

instruction.heading: Stopping spread during work
instruction.body: Stop cutting or moving any suspect plant as soon as you are unsure of its identity. Clean tools, gloves, boots and equipment before they leave the infected area, using the method approved by the business and suitable for the plant. Wash mower decks and trimmer heads, and brush soil and seed from boots and wheel rims. Do not blow leaves or clippings onto a footpath, into a drain or across a boundary into a neighbouring bushland or waterway. Use bagging, covered trailers and tarps where the material is at risk of falling or blowing away. Work from the cleanest area to the most infested area so that you do not carry seed across clean ground. Where the material cannot be controlled, stop and refer to the supervisor.

instruction.heading: Deciding what happens to the material
instruction.body: Once a plant is identified with confidence, you can decide what happens to the material, but only within the rules that apply. Ask four questions. Is the plant declared, restricted or otherwise regulated in this location? Can the material be moved off the property, and if so, what documents or containment are required? Is composting or chipping allowed, or will the material have to go to a specified disposal facility? Does the client or the land owner have a duty to report the plant? If you cannot answer every question from a reliable source, keep the material on site, contain it, and refer the decision. Do not state to the client that a plant is safe to compost or dispose of until the answer is confirmed.

instruction.heading: Verification and referral
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the reasoning, not just the final bag. A competent worker can explain what triggered the stop, how the plant was confirmed or left unconfirmed, what cleaning and containment were used, and who was informed. Good practice is a referral record with the species name if known, the location, the photographs taken, the containment used and the owner's notification. Do not certify that a site is free of an invasive plant. You can record that a plant was identified, controlled or referred, and what evidence supports that statement.

procedure: Before cutting, look at the plant's habit, leaves, flowers, seed and sap, and record any features that suggest a declared or restricted species.
If there is any uncertainty, stop cutting the plant, keep other material clear of it and mark its location.
Obtain a species identification from a reliable source, and record the source and the level of confidence.
Clean tools, gloves, boots and equipment before leaving the infected area, using the business's approved method.
Contain the material in bags, covered trailers or tarps and keep it separate from clean green waste.
Check the applicable state, territory and local rules for movement, composting, chipping and disposal before moving the material.
If the rules cannot be confirmed, keep the material on site, contain it and refer the decision to the supervisor and the owner.
Record the species, location, photographs, containment, disposal decision, owner notification and any referral.

workedExamples.situation: A neighbour says the climbing vine on the back fence is an invasive weed. The worker cannot confirm the species from the leaves alone, and the crew has already started cutting it.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the worker do with the vine and the cutting tools?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop cutting the vine, keep the cut stems away from clean green waste and mark the area. Clean the tools before moving to the next section of the garden. Obtain identification from a reliable source, record the uncertainty and inform the client. Do not compost, chip or move the vine until the identity and the local rule have been confirmed, and do not give the client a verbal assurance that it can be composted.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks the crew to take a large pile of cut ivy off the site to a green-waste collection point they use, and the trailer is already loaded.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the crew move the material, and what must happen first?
workedExamples.reasoning: The crew must not assume the material can be moved. Confirm the species, the movement limits for that location and the accepted disposal destination before the trailer leaves. If the ivy is confirmed as a regulated plant, the trailer must be covered and the destination must accept it. If the destination cannot be confirmed, the material stays on site in a contained area and the supervisor decides the next step with the client.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves suitable for handling thorny and sappy plants
Eye protection when cutting or clearing dense growth
Stiff brush, cleaning bucket and water for tools and boots
Heavy-duty bags, tarps and covered trailer for contained material
Identification guide or reference card for the local region
Camera or phone for recording the plant, with the client's consent

commonErrors.error: Identifying a suspect weed by eye and composting it with the clippings.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, contain and confirm identity from a reliable source before deciding on any disposal method.

commonErrors.error: Transporting a load in an open trailer to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Cover and secure the load. Check that the destination accepts that material before it leaves the site.

commonErrors.error: Moving from an infested area to a clean area without cleaning tools and boots.
commonErrors.prevention: Clean and inspect tools and footwear at the boundary of the infested zone, and work from clean to dirty where possible.

commonErrors.error: Telling the client a plant is safe to dispose of because it is common in the neighbourhood.
commonErrors.prevention: Only state what has been confirmed. Refer the disposal question and record what remains unconfirmed.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Declared and restricted plant lists, movement rules, reporting duties and disposal methods are set by each state or territory and by local government.

Some plant control and treatment methods, including herbicide use, need a licence or specific authority in some jurisdictions. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to treat a regulated plant.
Moving or disposing of regulated plant material without authority may be an offence. The applicable rule must be confirmed before transport.

Hazard controls for plant material are set out in the Safe Work Australia model framework, which requires risks to be managed so far as is reasonably practicable. This applies to handling plant hazards alongside biosecurity controls.

qualityStandard: No suspect plant material is cut, moved or composted until its identity and the applicable rule are confirmed or the material has been contained and referred.
Tools, gloves and boots are cleaned before leaving an infested area, and the cleaning method is recorded.
Each load of plant material has a documented destination that accepts that material.
Any uncertainty about species or rule is recorded and communicated to the client in writing.
documentationEvidence: Plant identification record: species name if known, source of identification, confidence level and photographs taken with consent.
Containment and cleaning record for tools, vehicles and boots.
Disposal or movement record with the destination, the load description and the receipt reference.
Referral and client notification record for any unresolved identity or disposal question.
summary: Plants spread through seed, cuttings, soil and equipment, so stop and contain when you are uncertain.
Identify from a reliable source. Do not identify by taste or touch.
Movement, composting and disposal rules are set by state, territory and local authorities, and must be confirmed before the material moves.
Record what was confirmed and what was referred. Do not certify that a site is free of invasive plants.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker is unsure whether a vine on a client's fence is a declared weed. What is the correct first step?
options: Cut the vine quickly and compost it, since most garden vines are harmless and add it to the compost bin today
Burn the vine on site to be sure it cannot spread and the smoke will not reach the neighbours or anyone
Stop cutting, keep the material separate and confirm the species from a reliable source before deciding on disposal.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before leaving an area with suspected invasive seed on the boots and tools, what should the worker do?
options: Clean the tools and boots using the approved method before moving to clean ground.
Shake the boots off on the footpath as they leave and walk on to the next site
Continue to the next site and clean the equipment at the end of the week.

knowledgeChecks.question: A load of cut plant material must go to a disposal destination. When can the crew load the trailer?
options: As soon as the trailer is available, since the destination will sort it out and the crew can leave the load uncovered
Once the material's identity, movement rule and an accepting destination have been confirmed, and the load is covered.
Once the client has signed a form saying the material is safe to move and the trailer has been checked by the crew
